tagline: District climate and planting signals from NASA data

footer.data: Data up to {to}. Site last built {built}.
footer.note: Demo build for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Field Shift). Weather values are NASA POWER model output (MERRA-2, about 50 km grid), not station readings. Advice is a signal to check with your local agriculture officer, not a prescription.

signal.aus: the date 10% of March–September rain has fallen
signal.aman: the date 40% of March–September rain has fallen

advice.earlier: In {district}, the rain pattern for {crop} has moved about {n} days earlier than in {a} ({signal}). Consider checking whether seedbeds and transplanting can move earlier, and confirm with your local agriculture officer.
advice.later: In {district}, the rain pattern for {crop} has moved about {n} days later than in {a} ({signal}). Consider checking whether seedbeds and transplanting can move later, and confirm with your local agriculture officer.
advice.none: For {crop} in {district}, we found no reliable shift in rain timing since {a}. Keep your usual planting calendar.
advice.boro-warmer: Winter nights in {district} have warmed by about {x} °C per decade since 1998. Boro seedlings may face less cold stress, but keep your usual calendar until your agriculture officer confirms.
advice.boro-cooler: Winter nights in {district} have cooled by about {x} °C per decade since 1998. Watch for cold stress on Boro seedlings and confirm timing with your agriculture officer.
advice.boro-none: For Boro in {district}, winter night temperatures show no reliable trend. Keep your usual planting calendar.

sms.earlier: {district}: {crop} rain has moved ~{n} days earlier. Check with the agri office.
sms.later: {district}: {crop} rain has moved ~{n} days later. Check with the agri office.
sms.none: {district}: no reliable change in {crop} rain timing. Keep your usual calendar.
sms.boro: {district}: Boro winter-night trend checked. See CropOrbit for details.

window.title: Planting window
window.lead: We compare two periods of the NASA record and report a shift only when the difference is clear and holds under different settings.
window.definition: Signal used: {signal}, counted from 1 March to 30 September.
window.smsLong: Longer than one message; it will be split.
window.caveatTitle: Read this before relying on it
window.caveat: We test 64 districts at once. By chance alone, about 6 would look significant. Across Bangladesh we found {k} flagged for Aman and {j} for Aus, which is close to what chance produces. Treat a flag as a reason to ask, never as a rule.
window.boroLead: Boro grows through winter, so rain timing is not the useful signal. We track winter night temperature and heat accumulation instead.
window.gdd: Heat accumulated in the season (growing degree days, base 10 °C)
window.thin: Significant means p below 0.10 and a shift of at least 2 days.

env.title: Environmental analysis
env.lead: Yearly values from the NASA record for this district's grid cell.
env.breakNote: The NASA model changed its inputs around 1998 and 2016, which moves rain, soil wetness, humidity and sunlight levels in steps. Those values are not comparable across the shaded years or the break lines. Temperature is shown from 1998 only.
env.noTrend: No trend is drawn for this measure because the steps above would create a false one.
env.monthlyNote: Rain and soil: median of {r1}–{r2}. Temperature: {t1}–{t2}.

unavail.title: Not available in this demo
unavail.hist: District-level crop area and yield records (for example from BBS or DAE) are not loaded in this demo, so we show no history rather than invent it. Below is what NASA data can add: how much heat each crop season accumulated.
unavail.forecast: A yield forecast needs district yield records and a model checked against held-back years. We have neither yet, so we show no number. The planting-window page is the supported tool for now.
unavail.next: What would unlock this: district crop statistics for at least 15 seasons, then a baseline that any model must beat.

about.title: Method and data
about.lead: Everything here comes from open data. This page says what was used, what was done to it, and where it can mislead.
about.d1: Weather: NASA POWER daily record (agroclimatology community), 1 January 1981 to {to}. POWER starts in 1981, so earlier years do not exist in this source.
about.d2: Boundaries: geoBoundaries (CC BY 4.0) via the bangladesh-geojson package, merged to 64 districts.
about.d3: Each district uses the nearest NASA grid cell (about 50 km). 64 districts share 45 cells.
about.d4: Freshness: the code repository includes a daily job that asks NASA POWER (no key needed) only for the newest days, re-runs the analysis and rebuilds the site. The newest days are provisional and NASA may revise them, so the job re-requests the last 120 days each time. Each district page also asks NASA directly for the last 30 days when you open it.
about.m1: Rain timing: the day by which a set share of March–September rain has fallen, compared between {a1}–{a2} and {b1}–{b2} with a rank test. The two periods are the 14 latest complete years and the 14 before them, so they move forward each year.
about.m2: A shift is reported only when p is below 0.10, the shift is at least 2 days, and the direction holds for a longer {la1}–{la2} vs {lb1}–{lb2} comparison and for stricter and looser settings.
about.m3: Temperature trends use 1998 onward only (Sen slope with Kendall test).
about.l1: POWER weather is a reanalysis model (MERRA-2), not station observation. Values can differ from your field.
about.l2: We measured step changes in the model around 1997/98 and 2016. Across 45 cells, yearly rain after 1998 is about {r1} times the level before, and after 2016 about {r2} times. Temperature falls by about {t1} °C at the first step. The cause is not confirmed, so long trends in rain and soil wetness are not drawn.
about.l3: With 64 districts, some flags appear by chance. See the planting-window page.
about.l4: No ML forecasting is included. It would need district crop data and validation we do not have.
about.o1: Code under Apache-2.0. AI assistance is disclosed in docs/AI_USE.md. Built by team FARMONAUTS.

iot.title: IoT irrigation demo
iot.lead: This shows the system we plan to build. Sensor readings, the radio link and the pump are simulated; the NASA rain signal is the real analysis for this district.
iot.concept: Concept demo. No hardware, radio or SMS is connected yet.
iot.how: How the real system would work

steps.1: Field sensors measure soil moisture, water-tank level and rain every few minutes.
steps.2: A low-power radio gateway (LoRa) collects the readings and sends them to the control centre over the mobile network (MQTT).
steps.3: The control centre adds the NASA POWER analysis for the district. If the last 30 days had less than half the usual rain, it starts irrigating earlier (start level raised by 5 points).
steps.4: If irrigation is needed and nothing blocks it (sensor fault, low tank, daily limit, rain expected), the centre sends a PUMP ON signal to the pump controller, and PUMP OFF when the target moisture is reached.
steps.5: The farmer gets an SMS at every start and stop and can override from a phone.

iot.nasaDry: NASA signal: last 30 days {a} mm against a usual {b} mm. Dry, so irrigation starts at {x}% instead of {y}%.
iot.nasaOk: NASA signal: last 30 days {a} mm against a usual {b} mm. No dry signal, so the standard start level of {x}% is used.
